input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.

Topic: CSCI-610: Foundations of Computer Graphics. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: Foundations of Computer Graphics is a study of the hardware and software principles of interactive raster graphics. Topics include an introduction to the basic concepts, 2-D and 3-D modeling and transformations, viewing transformations, projections, rendering techniques, graphical software packages and graphics systems. The course will focus on rasterization techniques and emphasize the hardware rasterization pipeline including the use of hardware shaders. Students will use a standard computer graphics API to reinforce concepts and study fundamental computer graphics algorithms. Programming projects and a survey of the current graphics literature will be required. Note: students who complete CSCI-510 may not take CSCI-610 for credit. Prerequisite: (CSCI-603 or CSCI-605 with a grade of B or better) or (CSCI-243 or SWEN-262). May not take and receive credit for CSCI-610 and CSCI-510. If earned credit for/or currently enrolled in CSCI-510 you will not be permitted to enroll in CSCI-610. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring

Source excerpts:

[khronos-opengl]
The OpenGL graphics pipeline processes vertices through programmable shader stages. Primitive assembly groups vertices into points, lines, or triangles. Clipping removes portions outside the view volume. Rasterization converts primitives into fragment candidates. Interpolation produces per-fragment values from vertex outputs. Fragment processing computes values for framebuffer operations. Depth testing resolves visibility according to stored depth values. Blending combines a fragment result with an existing framebuffer value. Coordinate spaces, sampling, and numerical precision must remain explicit.

[mit-computer-graphics]
Computer graphics uses geometric models to represent objects and scenes. Transformations position and orient geometry within coordinate systems. Viewing maps a scene through a camera model to an image. Rasterization samples projected primitives on a discrete pixel grid. Shading models how light, material, and geometry determine appearance. Texture mapping associates image data with geometric surfaces. Curves and surfaces provide compact smooth shape representations. Animation changes scene state over time. Ray tracing follows visibility and light paths through a scene. Visual correctness follows from explicit conventions, assumptions, sampling decisions, and measurable error.

beats.claim: The OpenGL graphics pipeline processes vertices through programmable shader stages before rasterization.
beats.example: A triangle mesh is passed to vertex shaders that compute position and normal attributes for each vertex.
beats.title: Introduction to Raster Graphics Pipeline
beats.visualDirection: Display a flowchart showing vertex input -> vertex shader -> primitive assembly -> clipping -> rasterization -> fragment shader -> framebuffer.

beats.claim: Primitive assembly groups vertices into points, lines, or triangles, and clipping removes portions outside the view volume.
beats.example: A polygon with one vertex outside the camera frustum is clipped to intersect the view volume boundaries.
beats.title: Primitive Assembly and Clipping
beats.visualDirection: Show a 3-D polygon being clipped by a view frustum, highlighting the clipped-out segment and the resulting clipped primitive.

beats.claim: Rasterization converts primitives into fragment candidates, and interpolation produces per-fragment values from vertex outputs.
beats.example: A triangle is rasterized into a set of pixels, with color and normal values interpolated across each pixel based on barycentric coordinates.
beats.title: Rasterization and Interpolation
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a triangle being rasterized into a grid of pixels, with color gradients showing interpolated vertex attributes.

beats.claim: Fragment processing computes values for framebuffer operations, and depth testing resolves visibility according to stored depth values.
beats.example: A backface-occluded triangle is discarded because its depth value is greater than the stored depth buffer value at that pixel.
beats.title: Fragment Processing and Depth Testing
beats.visualDirection: Show a depth buffer comparison where a closer triangle overwrites a farther triangle's pixel values.

beats.claim: Blending combines a fragment result with an existing framebuffer value, and coordinate spaces, sampling, and numerical precision must remain explicit.
beats.example: A semi-transparent overlay is blended with the underlying scene using alpha blending to produce a final pixel color.
beats.title: Blending and Coordinate Spaces
beats.visualDirection: Demonstrate alpha blending by showing a transparent shape merging with a solid background, highlighting the alpha channel calculation.

beats.claim: Computer graphics uses geometric models to represent objects and scenes, and transformations position and orient geometry within coordinate systems.
beats.example: A 3-D model is translated, rotated, and scaled using transformation matrices to position it in the scene.
beats.title: Geometric Modeling and Transformations
beats.visualDirection: Show a 3-D object being transformed through space, with axes and matrix values displayed alongside the transformed geometry.

beats.claim: Viewing maps a scene through a camera model to an image, and projections convert 3-D coordinates into 2-D image plane coordinates.
beats.example: A perspective projection matrix converts 3-D world coordinates into 2-D screen coordinates, simulating camera depth.
beats.title: Viewing and Projection
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a camera model projecting 3-D scene geometry onto a 2-D image plane, showing the projection matrix in action.

beats.claim: Shading models how light, material, and geometry determine appearance, and texture mapping associates image data with geometric surfaces.
beats.example: A diffuse shading model computes surface brightness based on light direction and surface normal, while a texture map applies a 2-D image to a 3-D surface.
beats.title: Shading and Texture Mapping
beats.visualDirection: Show a 3-D surface with diffuse shading and a texture overlay, highlighting the light direction and normal vector calculations.

beats.claim: The course emphasizes the hardware rasterization pipeline including the use of hardware shaders to process fragment data efficiently.
beats.example: A fragment shader computes lighting and color values for each pixel in parallel on the GPU, accelerating rasterization.
beats.title: Hardware Shaders and Rasterization Focus
beats.visualDirection: Display a GPU architecture diagram highlighting shader cores processing fragment data during the rasterization stage.

beats.claim: Visual correctness follows from explicit conventions, assumptions, sampling decisions, and measurable error in rendering pipelines.
beats.example: A renderer checks anti-aliasing, depth precision, and sampling rates to ensure measurable error remains within acceptable bounds.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Show a checklist graphic with items like 'Verify depth buffer precision', 'Check sampling rates', 'Validate coordinate transformations', and 'Measure visual error'.

learningObjectives: Define the core components of the hardware rasterization pipeline and explain their sequential processing of geometric primitives.
Apply coordinate transformations and projection matrices to map 3-D scene geometry into a 2-D image plane for rendering.
Evaluate the role of hardware shaders and rasterization techniques in determining visual correctness and performance in interactive graphics.
